title: Syrah
description: Also called Shiraz. Pepper and smoke in the Rhône, ripe dark fruit in the Barossa.
L: Describe Syrah's colour, aromas and structure

Syrah is a thick-skinned black grape giving deep purple wines with blackberry, blueberry and plum, plus black pepper, smoked meat, olive and violet. Tannins are firm but usually ripe, acidity medium to high. Ripe examples add chocolate and liquorice. It's one of the world's most planted red grapes.

DNA shows Syrah is a natural cross of two grapes from south-east France: Dureza, from the Ardèche, and Mondeuse Blanche, from Savoie. Its black pepper aroma comes from rotundone, a compound also found in peppercorns. Rotundone forms most in cooler sites and vintages; about one in five people can't smell it at all.
What compound gives Syrah its black pepper aroma?
Rotundone is the same compound found in black peppercorns. Pyrazines give green pepper, not black.

Look for deep purple, almost opaque colour. On the nose, dark fruit with pepper or smoky, meaty notes suggests Syrah. On the palate, firm but ripe tannins and a savoury finish. Cooler examples are peppery and medium-bodied; warmer ones are fuller, sweeter-fruited and chocolatey.
Dark colour plus pepper or smoke
Syrah is a cross between two grapes from south-east France.
Yes. Its parents are Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche, both from the area around the Rhône and the Alps.
Syrah gives dark fruit, black pepper and smoky, meaty notes
It's a cross of Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche
Rotundone gives its pepper aroma, most in cooler sites
From the Rhône to the world

Syrah's classic home is the northern Rhône, on steep granite slopes. It is also a key grape in the southern Rhône and the Languedoc, blended with Grenache and Mourvèdre. As Shiraz, it is Australia's most planted grape. It grows in South Africa, California, Washington, Chile, Argentina and New Zealand's Hawke's Bay.

Syrah needs warmth to ripen, but not extreme heat: too hot, and it loses acidity and turns jammy. Moderate climates give the most aromatic wines, with pepper and violet. Warm climates give richer, fuller, more alcoholic wines. It tolerates drought reasonably well, but its shoots can break in strong wind, like the Mistral.
Moderate for pepper; warm for richness
Match each region to its Syrah style.
The same grape shifts style with climate and tradition.

In the southern Rhône and Australia, Syrah joins Grenache and Mourvèdre in GSM blends, adding colour and structure. In Côte-Rôtie, a little white Viognier may be co-fermented with it, lifting aroma and stabilising colour. In Australia, a Shiraz Cabernet blend is a classic, invented there.
Which white grape is sometimes co-fermented with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie?
Up to 20% Viognier is allowed in Côte-Rôtie, though most use far less.
Syrah grows in the Rhône, Australia and much of the New World
Moderate climates give pepper; warm ones give richness
It blends with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier and Cabernet
Explain why it makes such distinct Syrah

The northern Rhône runs about 60 km along the river, from Vienne to Valence. Vineyards cling to steep granite slopes, often on terraces held by stone walls. The climate is continental, cooler than the south. Syrah is the only red grape allowed, sometimes with a little white Viognier, Marsanne or Roussanne.

Côte-Rôtie, meaning roasted slope, makes perfumed, elegant Syrah. Hermitage, a single hill facing south, makes powerful, long-lived wines. Cornas makes dark, rustic, firm wines. Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage are larger, more affordable areas. Crozes-Hermitage is the biggest, with flatter vineyards.
Match each appellation to its style.
Each northern Rhône appellation shows a different face of Syrah.
Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph offer a taste of northern Rhône Syrah at a fraction of Hermitage's price. Look for producers who also make wines from the famous hills.
In the northern Rhône, Syrah is often blended with Grenache.
Not true. Syrah is the only red grape in the northern Rhône. Grenache belongs to the southern Rhône.
The northern Rhône grows Syrah on steep granite slopes
Côte-Rôtie is perfumed; Hermitage powerful; Cornas rustic
Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph are more affordable
Explain the role of old vines
Explain how Penfolds Grange changed Australian wine

The Barossa Valley, north-east of Adelaide, is warm and dry. Shiraz there is full-bodied, around 14.5 to 15% alcohol, with ripe blackberry, plum, chocolate, liquorice and often American oak's vanilla and coconut. Tannins are soft and ripe. It's the style that made Australian Shiraz famous worldwide.

Phylloxera never reached South Australia, so the Barossa has some of the oldest Shiraz vines in the world, some planted in the 1840s by Silesian settlers. Old vines give low yields and concentrated fruit. The Barossa Old Vine Charter classifies Old Vines at 35 years and Ancestor vines at 125 years or more.
Why does the Barossa have such old Shiraz vines?
Strict quarantine kept phylloxera out, so the original ungrafted vines survive.

In 1951, Max Schubert, Penfolds' chief winemaker, made an experimental Shiraz after visiting Bordeaux. Penfolds Grange, aged in new American oak, was first mocked, then celebrated. It became Australia's most famous wine and showed that Shiraz could make world-class, long-lived wines.
Barossa Shiraz is deeply coloured and full, not pale.
Barossa Shiraz is ripe, full and chocolatey
Old ungrafted vines date back to the 1840s
Penfolds Grange, from 1951, made Australian Shiraz world-class
Explain where the name Shiraz came from

Syrah and Shiraz are the same grape. Shiraz is the name used in Australia and South Africa, possibly from an old local spelling. A popular legend links it to the Persian city of Shiraz, but DNA proves the grape is French. James Busby brought cuttings to Australia in 1832.

Today, many producers choose the name to signal style. Syrah suggests a cooler, Rhône-like wine: peppery, savoury, medium-bodied. Shiraz suggests a riper, fuller, fruit-forward wine. Some cool-climate Australian producers now label their wines Syrah for this reason.
James Busby brought Syrah cuttings to Australia in ____.
Busby's collection in 1832 included Syrah, which became Australia's Shiraz.

Australia isn't only warm. The Yarra Valley, Canberra District, Great Southern and Adelaide Hills make lighter, peppery Shiraz. Canberra is known for Shiraz co-fermented with Viognier, inspired by Côte-Rôtie. These wines show that Australia's Shiraz can be elegant as well as powerful.
An Australian wine is labelled Syrah instead of Shiraz. What does this most likely signal?
Many producers use Syrah to signal a cooler, Rhône-like style.
Syrah and Shiraz are the same French grape
The name often signals style: peppery Syrah, ripe Shiraz
Australia's cooler regions make elegant, peppery Shiraz
Serve it at the right temperature

Syrah's dark fruit and pepper suit grilled and roasted meat: lamb, beef, game and barbecue. Peppery Rhône styles match herbs and black pepper crust. Ripe Barossa Shiraz handles sweet, smoky barbecue sauces. Avoid very delicate dishes, which it overwhelms.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Young, powerful Syrah benefits from decanting. Good Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie age 15 to 30 years, developing leather, game and earthy notes. Top Barossa Shiraz also ages well. Simpler Shiraz is best within a few years.
Which dish suits a peppery northern Rhône Syrah?
Lamb with rosemary and black pepper
Herbs and pepper echo the wine's own aromas; lamb's fat softens its tannins.

Syrah also makes rosé, sparkling red Shiraz, a beloved Australian Christmas wine, and fortified styles in Australia. In blends, it's part of Côtes du Rhône and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Learning to taste for its pepper is one of the most useful skills in blind tasting.
Sparkling red Shiraz is a traditional Australian style.
Yes. It's often served with Christmas lunch in Australia.
Syrah suits lamb, game and barbecue
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees; the best age for decades
It also makes rosé and sparkling red Shiraz
